lessons.title: The riff is the progression
explanation: Treat the riff as the progression. The cell's letters, intervals, and return are the harmony. A chord chart you invent after the fact — four Roman numerals that never get struck as chords — is a second piece. Analyze the piece that was played.

Power chords, pedals, and chromatic neighbors can be the whole harmonic story of a section. MIT 21M.350 still asks what repeats. Answer with the cell, not with a chorale reduction that stacks SATB on a palm mute. If the guitar plays E–F–E, that is the progression.

Write a two-bar cell and refuse to 'realize' it as i–ii°–i. Name the cell, the interval content, and where it returns. A chart is allowed only when those chords are actually voiced. Otherwise the riff is the chart.
lessons.example: Palm-muted E–F–Gb–F, two bars, no other guitar. The progression is that chromatic cell. A chart that writes Em–F–Gb+–F invents qualities the riff never voiced.
lessons.whyItMatters: Invent a chorale and you will rehearse voicings nobody tracked. Analyze the cell and you can write the next one.

quiz.stem: Treating the riff as the progression means you should report which object?
quiz.correctAnswer: The cell's letters, intervals, and return as the harmony

distractors.text: A Roman-numeral chart invented so the riff can look like a chorale
distractors.rationale: The invented chart is a second piece.

distractors.text: Only the drum pattern, because riffs cannot carry harmony
distractors.rationale: The cell is harmonic material.

distractors.text: The mix fader position at the start of each bar
distractors.rationale: Loudness is not the progression.

quiz.correctExplanation: What the guitar strikes is the progression. Report that.
objectiveIds: Treat the riff as the progression

quiz.stem: A section is a repeating E–F–E cell. Analyzing by an invented i–ii–i chart is a mistake because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The chart names chords the riff never voiced; the cell was the harmony

distractors.text: E–F–E cannot be harmonic until someone adds a third on top
distractors.rationale: The two-note cell is already the progression.

distractors.text: Analysis is banned in riff music, so no report should exist
distractors.rationale: Report the cell. That is the analysis.

distractors.text: The letters must be rewritten as C major before a chart can speak
distractors.rationale: Relative-major rescue is another invention.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the chords were not struck, they are not the section.
objectiveIds: Analyze a section by the cell, not by a chord chart you invented

quiz.stem: You transcribe a palm-muted two-bar cell with no chord stabs. Honest analysis should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Name the cell and refuse a chord chart those attacks never played

distractors.text: Stack SATB on the mute so a chorale can replace the riff
distractors.rationale: SATB on a mute is the invented second piece.

distractors.text: Delete the pitches and keep only beaming, because cells are rhythm only
distractors.rationale: Letters are half of the cell.

distractors.text: Force a V–I at the barline so the cell can graduate to a phrase
distractors.rationale: A cadence the riff skipped is not the cell.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cell, interval content, return. That is the section's harmony.
objectiveIds: Analyze a section by the cell, not by a chord chart you invented

lessons.title: Open string everything else grinds against
explanation: Hold an open string while the figures above it change. The pedal is a tonic drone, a grinding post, not a missing chord tone waiting to be named. Clashes happen when the moving figure leaves the unison or the fifth. Release happens when it comes back.

Write the grind on purpose: F against an E pedal, then Gb, then back to E. Each clash is a measured dissonance against a fixed pitch. If the open string stops whenever the figure moves, you wrote changing roots, not a pedal riff.

A useful pedal riff lets the clash last long enough to hear, then releases. MIT 21M.302 still knows a pedal as a held tone under changing harmony. Here the changing 'harmony' is the riff cell. Keep the open string ringing through the neighbors.
lessons.example: Open low E through a whole bar. Fretted F, Gb, F, E on the next string. The E never lifts. F and Gb clash; E releases. Lift the open string on the Gb and the pedal job ends.
lessons.whyItMatters: Lift the drone when the figure moves and you lose the grind. The clashes need a wall that stays.

quiz.stem: Grinding changing figures against an open string requires which of these to stay put?
quiz.correctAnswer: The open pitch, ringing while neighbors leave and return

distractors.text: The open pitch, muted the moment the figure leaves unison
distractors.rationale: Muting ends the pedal and the grind.

distractors.text: A new open string for every neighbor, so nothing can clash
distractors.rationale: One wall. Many neighbors.

distractors.text: The snare only, because pedals are a drum technique here
distractors.rationale: The pedal is a held pitch.

quiz.correctExplanation: The wall stays. The figure moves. That is the grind.
objectiveIds: Grind changing figures against an open string

quiz.stem: A pedal riff whose clashes release should do which of these jobs?
quiz.correctAnswer: Let neighbors bite the open string, then return to unison or fifth

distractors.text: Keep every neighbor forever so release is banned as too consonant
distractors.rationale: Release is part of the writing.

distractors.text: Change the open string to match each neighbor and cancel clashes
distractors.rationale: Matching cancels the pedal.

distractors.text: Resolve each clash through a dominant of the neighbor pitch
distractors.rationale: The release is return to the wall, not a cadence.

quiz.correctExplanation: Clash, then return. The open string is still there for both.
objectiveIds: Write a pedal riff whose clashes release

quiz.stem: The open E stops whenever the figure plays F. Diagnose the writing:
quiz.correctAnswer: The drone lifted, so the F is a new root rather than a grind

distractors.text: The pedal got stronger, because silence proves the E is still home
distractors.rationale: Silence is not a pedal.

distractors.text: The clash released by becoming a tritone substitution of E
distractors.rationale: No E sounded. There was no wall to grind.

distractors.text: Form changed to verse-chorus because a mute is a section break
distractors.rationale: The issue is the missing drone, not form labels.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the wall leaves with the figure, you wrote changing roots.
objectiveIds: Write a pedal riff whose clashes release

lessons.title: Semitone motion as the material
explanation: Semitone motion can be the riff, not a passing tone on the way to a 'real' chord. A two-note cell E–F, sequenced up or down, is already the material. Decorating a pentatonic skeleton with one chromatic neighbor is a different job. Here the half-steps are the skeleton.

Sequence the cell without turning it into a scale run. E–F, then F–Gb, then Gb–G is a sequenced two-note unit. E–F–F#–G–Ab–A as one smear is a run. The difference is whether you can still point to the two-note object that repeats.

Write three sequences of a descending E–Eb cell, then stop. Do not fill the leftover frets 'to complete the chromatic scale.' Completing the scale erases the cell. MIT analysis would still ask what repeats: the two-note unit, or a pan up the neck.
lessons.example: E–F, then D#–E, then D–D#, each pair an eighth-eighth. Three cells. A six-note chromatic sweep on the same beats is the run this lesson refuses.
lessons.whyItMatters: If the half-steps are only decoration, a diatonic rewrite will not hurt. If they are the cell, that rewrite deletes the piece.

quiz.stem: Using semitone motion as the material, not the decoration, means which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: The half-step cell is the riff's skeleton, not a neighbor on a diatonic frame

distractors.text: One chromatic passing tone on an otherwise pentatonic riff
distractors.rationale: That passing tone is decoration, not the skeleton.

distractors.text: A ban on half-steps so only whole tones can be material
distractors.rationale: Half-steps are the material here.

distractors.text: A mix-fader sweep that only sounds like pitch motion
distractors.rationale: The frets move by semitone. That is pitch.

quiz.correctExplanation: The cell is E–F, or whatever half-step you chose. That is the riff.
objectiveIds: Use semitone motion as the material, not the decoration

quiz.stem: Sequencing a two-note chromatic cell without a scale run looks like which writing?
quiz.correctAnswer: Repeat the pair at new starting frets, keeping the two-note object audible

distractors.text: Fill every fret in a row so the neck becomes one smear
distractors.rationale: The smear is the run this lesson refuses.

distractors.text: Hold one pitch and decorate it with random chromatic grace notes
distractors.rationale: Grace notes are ornaments, not a sequenced cell.

distractors.text: Replace the pair with a seven-note minor scale in eighths
distractors.rationale: A scale run is a different object.

quiz.correctExplanation: Point to the pair. If you cannot, you wrote a run.
objectiveIds: Sequence a two-note chromatic cell without turning it into a scale run

quiz.stem: A chart 'completes' your E–F sequences into a full chromatic scale. Diagnose it:
quiz.correctAnswer: The extra notes erased the two-note cell that was the material

distractors.text: The completion proved the cell was only decoration all along
distractors.rationale: The cell was the skeleton. Completion buried it.

distractors.text: Chromatic scales are required before any half-step can count
distractors.rationale: Two notes already count.

distractors.text: The chart only changed loudness, so the cell is still intact
distractors.rationale: New letters were added. That is pitch.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the repeating object is gone, the riff is gone.
objectiveIds: Sequence a two-note chromatic cell without turning it into a scale run

lessons.title: Seconds stacked until the name fails
explanation: Stack seconds until the chord has no common-practice name. E–F–G–Ab in one fist is a cluster, not a misspelled dominant. Close dissonance is a voicing choice: the bite is the interval packing, not a wrong inversion of a triad you wished had been there.

Decide whether that cluster is the harmony or a passing smear. If it sits for a bar and returns, it is a chord the riff owns. If it is a rake into an E5, it is a smear. MIT analysis still asks what repeats. A smear does not repeat as an object. A cluster-harmony does.

Write a two-beat cluster, then either hold it as the section's home voicing or spill it into a fifth. Do not respell it as C7b9 just to give the page a textbook label. If no one voiced C7, the name is a costume.
lessons.example: Left-hand cluster E–F–G held under a vocal. That is the harmony. The same three notes raked in a 32nd-note slide into E5 is a smear into a fifth.
lessons.whyItMatters: Name a cluster as a broken seventh and you will 'resolve' a chord the band is using as home. Decide the job first.

quiz.stem: Stacking seconds until the chord has no common-practice name produces which object?
quiz.correctAnswer: A cluster whose bite is the packed intervals, not a misspelled triad

distractors.text: A dominant seventh that is hiding and must be respelled as V
distractors.rationale: If no one voiced V, the name is a costume.

distractors.text: A rest, because unnamed chords are legally silent
distractors.rationale: The cluster still sounds.

distractors.text: A power chord with extra gain that only looks like seconds
distractors.rationale: Seconds are pitch packing, not a gain knob.

quiz.correctExplanation: Packed seconds. No textbook nickname required.
objectiveIds: Stack seconds until the chord has no common-practice name

quiz.stem: A cluster that sits for a bar and returns, versus a rake into E5, should be distinguished as:
quiz.correctAnswer: Harmony if it repeats as an object; smear if it only leads into another chord

distractors.text: Always harmony, because any dissonance is a tonic by law
distractors.rationale: Job depends on whether the cluster is the object.

distractors.text: Always a smear, because clusters cannot be harmonic material
distractors.rationale: A held, returning cluster is material.

distractors.text: A meter change, because stacked seconds regroup the bar
distractors.rationale: This is voicing, not grouping.

quiz.correctExplanation: What repeats is the harmony. What only passes is a smear.
objectiveIds: Decide whether that cluster is the harmony or a passing smear

quiz.stem: Holding a cluster as home versus using it as a pickup is which tradeoff?
quiz.correctAnswer: Home cluster costs a named triad; smear keeps a target chord and spends the bite

distractors.text: Both jobs require respelling the cluster as a chorale V–I
distractors.rationale: Respell is the costume this lesson refuses.

distractors.text: Home clusters forbid return, so they cannot be form
distractors.rationale: Return is how a cluster proves it is harmony.

distractors.text: Smears must last a full section or they do not count as dissonance
distractors.rationale: A smear is short by job, not by law.

quiz.correctExplanation: Choose the job. Home or pickup. The packing is the same intervals.
objectiveIds: Decide whether that cluster is the harmony or a passing smear

lessons.title: Contrast and return without verse-chorus
explanation: Form from riffs is contrast and return of cells. Section B can be a new cell, or the old cell displaced, or the old cell under a new kit texture. You mark the change where the repeating object changes.

A drum texture swap with a new cell is already a section. You do not owe a chorus lyric or a lift into relative major. MIT 21M.350 still asks what contrasts. If the cell and the kit both change, that is a boundary. If only the vocal enters, you may still be in the same riff-section.

Build A as cell X for eight bars, B as cell Y plus blast or half-time, then return to X. That ABA is form. Writing 'verse' on A and 'chorus' on B does not add a mechanism. It adds a costume from a map the music did not use.
lessons.example: Cell X, open hat, four bars. Cell Y, closed hat and a new kick map, four bars. Back to X. The boundary is the new cell plus the kit. No chorus lift is required for the return to count.
lessons.whyItMatters: Wait for a chorus that never arrives and you will miss the actual boundaries. Mark cell and texture. That is the map.

quiz.stem: Building form from contrast and return of cells, not verse-chorus, means which map?
quiz.correctAnswer: Section boundaries where the repeating cell or its contrast changes

distractors.text: A required chorus lift into relative major before any section can count
distractors.rationale: No chorus contract is owed.

distractors.text: A single cell for the whole track, because return forbids contrast
distractors.rationale: Return needs something to return from.

distractors.text: Bar numbers only, with cells ignored as mere pitch decoration
distractors.rationale: The cell is what form is made of here.

quiz.correctExplanation: What repeats, what contrasts, what returns. That is the form.
objectiveIds: Build form from contrast and return of cells, not from verse-chorus

quiz.stem: A section change that is only a drum texture and a new cell should be marked as:
quiz.correctAnswer: A real boundary: new repeating object plus a new kit gait

distractors.text: Not a section, because no chorus lyric arrived to certify it
distractors.rationale: Lyric costume is not the mechanism.

distractors.text: A modulation, because kit changes always mean a new tonic
distractors.rationale: Texture and cell moved. Key can sit.

distractors.text: An intro forever, because odd textures cannot leave the opening
distractors.rationale: A new cell in the middle is a middle section.

quiz.correctExplanation: New cell, new kit. You already have a section change.
objectiveIds: Mark a section change that is only a drum texture and a new cell

quiz.stem: Cell X, then cell Y with half-time, then X again. Compared with verse-chorus labels, this is:
quiz.correctAnswer: ABA by cell and texture; the labels would only costume the same map

distractors.text: Not form, because ABA is illegal without a sung chorus
distractors.rationale: Return of X is already form.

distractors.text: Verse-chorus in disguise, so Y must be rewritten as a hook
distractors.rationale: Y is a contrasting cell, not a owed hook.

distractors.text: Through-composed chaos, because riffs cannot return on purpose
distractors.rationale: The return of X is the purpose.

quiz.correctExplanation: Contrast, then return. Name the cells. Skip the costume.
objectiveIds: Build form from contrast and return of cells, not from verse-chorus

lessons.title: What repeats, what contrasts, what is the cell
explanation: Ask three questions before you name a theory: what repeats, what contrasts, and what is the cell. The cell is the smallest object that still explains the section when you point at it. If you cannot point, you do not have a cell yet. You have a fog of notes.

Refuse an analysis that invents a chorale the music does not play. SATB on a two-note mute, or a V–I the guitar skipped, is a second piece. MIT 21M.350 is a method for saying what a work does. Use it on riffs. Do not use it as a machine that outputs Bach.

Work a section: circle the repeating pitch-rhythm object, mark where a new object or texture enters, and stop. If a Roman numeral helps because those chords were voiced, keep it. If it only makes the page look like a harmony exam, cut it.
lessons.example: Two-bar E–F cell, eight times; then a three-note chromatic cell under half-time. The analysis is: cell X repeats, cell Y contrasts, kit gait contrasts. No chorale.
lessons.whyItMatters: Start from a theory nickname and you will force the tape to match the nickname. Start from the cell and the theory has to match the tape.

quiz.stem: The first three questions of this method, in the job they do, are which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: What repeats, what contrasts, and what object is the cell

distractors.text: What key, what cadence, and which chorale the riff secretly is
distractors.rationale: Those questions invent a second piece.

distractors.text: What plugin, what decade, and which band to name-drop
distractors.rationale: The method is about the sounding object.

distractors.text: What tempo only, because riffs cannot repeat pitch on purpose
distractors.rationale: Pitch-rhythm cells repeat. Ask that too.

quiz.correctExplanation: Repeat, contrast, cell. Point at the object or you do not have it.
objectiveIds: Ask what repeats, what contrasts, and what the cell is

quiz.stem: An analysis that stacks SATB and a V–I on a two-note mute should be refused because:
quiz.correctAnswer: It invents a chorale the music does not play

distractors.text: All analysis is banned, so even naming the cell is illegal
distractors.rationale: Name the cell. Refuse the invented chorale.

distractors.text: SATB is required; the mute must be rewritten until it cadences
distractors.rationale: Rewriting is the invention.

distractors.text: Two-note mutes cannot repeat, so contrast is the only legal question
distractors.rationale: The mute can be the repeating cell.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the chorale was not played, it is not the analysis.
objectiveIds: Refuse an analysis that invents a chorale the music does not play

quiz.stem: Integrating the method on a section with cell X then cell Y means you should report:
quiz.correctAnswer: X repeats, Y contrasts, and both cells named without an invented chorale

distractors.text: A single Roman-numeral paragraph that replaces both cells
distractors.rationale: Replacement is the second piece.

distractors.text: Only the kit, because cells are too small to count as form
distractors.rationale: Cells are what form is made of here.

distractors.text: A modulation chart into the relative major of whichever cell is louder
distractors.rationale: Loudness does not elect a chorale key.

quiz.correctExplanation: Point at X. Point at Y. Do not dress them as SATB.
objectiveIds: Ask what repeats, what contrasts, and what the cell is

lessons.title: A method that starts from the cell
explanation: MIT 21M.350 trains a habit: say what the work does before you say what school it belongs to. On riff music that habit starts at the cell. Pitch plus rhythm, short enough to point at, long enough that repeating it still is the section. If your object is 'the song is Phrygian,' you skipped the cell and jumped to a nickname.

Repeat and contrast are operations, not moods. A cell that comes back unchanged is a return. A cell that comes back displaced is a variation. A new cell under a new kit texture is a contrast. Write those operations in that order. A paragraph of genre adjectives is not a substitute for the list.

Refuse the invented chorale in detail. Common-practice tools still help when the music uses them: a voiced triad, an actual dominant, a pedal that behaves like a textbook pedal. They fail when you stack inner voices the guitar never played, or when you complete a cadence to make the phrase 'correct.' Cut anything the tape does not support.

A finished report names the cell, lists what repeats and what contrasts, notes meter and timbre when they are harmonic facts, and stops. It does not award moral ranks to intervals. It does not rescue the riff into a key it refused. The method is done when another player could rebuild the section from your notes.
lessons.example: Cell X: E–F eighths, two bars. Repeats four times. Contrast: X displaced one eighth, then cell Y (E–Bb) under half-time. Timbre: the fifth under gain is a crowd, not a clean triad. No V–I. That paragraph is the analysis.
lessons.whyItMatters: A method you can rerun beats a nickname you cannot check. Start from the cell or you will analyze a chorale that was never tracked.

quiz.stem: Starting from the cell, a report that another player could rebuild should contain which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: The pointed-at object, what repeats, what contrasts, and no unsupported cadence

distractors.text: A school nickname first, then a chorale that makes the nickname true
distractors.rationale: Nickname-first is the habit the method drops.

distractors.text: Only plugin names and a decade, because cells cannot be written down
distractors.rationale: The cell is the writable object.

distractors.text: A complete SATB realization so the riff can pass a species exam
distractors.rationale: Species on a mute is the invented chorale.

quiz.correctExplanation: Point, list operations, stop. That is a rebuildable report.
objectiveIds: Ask what repeats, what contrasts, and what the cell is

quiz.stem: When do common-practice labels still belong in this method, and when do you refuse them?
quiz.correctAnswer: Keep them if those chords were voiced; refuse them if they invent a chorale

distractors.text: Always keep V–I, because analysis is the completing of cadences
distractors.rationale: Completing cadences is the invention.

distractors.text: Always refuse every triad name, even when a triad was struck
distractors.rationale: Struck triads can keep their names.

distractors.text: Keep them only for the kit, because drums are the true harmony
distractors.rationale: Labels track sounding pitch, not a drum ethic.

quiz.correctExplanation: Supported by the tape: keep. Invented SATB: cut.
objectiveIds: Refuse an analysis that invents a chorale the music does not play

quiz.stem: A report that awards moral ranks to intervals and rescues a riff into a refused key is which tradeoff failure?
quiz.correctAnswer: It traded a rebuildable method for a nickname the tape does not support

distractors.text: It gained accuracy, because ranks and rescues are what analysis is for
distractors.rationale: Accuracy is matching the tape, not ranking it.

distractors.text: It only failed if the nickname was Phrygian rather than Locrian
distractors.rationale: The failure is nickname-first, not which nickname.

distractors.text: It succeeded as long as the cell was mentioned in a footnote
distractors.rationale: A footnote cell still lost to the rescue.

quiz.correctExplanation: Method first. Nickname only if the cell still matches after you check.
objectiveIds: Refuse an analysis that invents a chorale the music does not play

lessons.title: Strip the surface, keep the riff
explanation: Strip doublings, fills, and pickup smears until the remaining object still explains the riff. That leftover is the reduction. If the leftover is a I–V the guitar never played, you did not reduce. You replaced. MIT 21M.350 still reduces; it does not get to invent a chorale on the way down.

A honest reduction of a pedal riff is the pedal plus the moving cell, not a triad cycle. A honest reduction of a chromatic cell is the two-note unit and its sequence path. Extra inner voices that 'complete' the stack belong on the cutting-room floor unless they were tracked.

Leave a reduction another player could use to rebuild the section. If they would rebuild a cadence the tape skipped, your reduction failed. Keep meter grouping if the addends were the form. Drop a lead fill that never returns. The test is still: does this explain the riff that was played?
lessons.example: Surface: E5 doubled, a 32nd rake, then E–F–E cell with a harmonic squeal. Reduction: E pedal, E–F cell, 3+2+2 grouping. Not Em–B7. The squeal and the rake do not survive.
lessons.whyItMatters: A reduction that invents I–V will teach the next player the wrong piece. Strip until the riff is still there, then stop.

quiz.stem: Stripping the surface without inventing a I–V that is not there means you should keep what?
quiz.correctAnswer: The sounding cell and pedal, not a cadence the guitar skipped

distractors.text: A I–V skeleton, because every riff secretly cadences underneath
distractors.rationale: A skipped cadence is not a reduction; it is a replacement.

distractors.text: Every fill and rake, because reduction is forbidden to cut anything
distractors.rationale: Fills that never return are surface.

distractors.text: Only the kit click, because pitch cannot survive a reduction
distractors.rationale: The cell is pitch. It should survive.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cut the extra. Do not add a handshake the tape omitted.
objectiveIds: Strip the surface without inventing a I–V that is not there

quiz.stem: A reduction of a chromatic E–F cell that comes out Em–B7 should be diagnosed as:
quiz.correctAnswer: A replacement chorale, not a stripping that still explains the riff

distractors.text: A success, because I–V is the only legal leftover of any riff
distractors.rationale: I–V was not on the tape.

distractors.text: A meter reduction, because Roman numerals secretly group 7/8
distractors.rationale: The error is harmonic invention, not grouping.

distractors.text: An incomplete reduction that still needs more inner voices added
distractors.rationale: Adding voices is the opposite of stripping.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the leftover is a cadence nobody played, you replaced the riff.
objectiveIds: Strip the surface without inventing a I–V that is not there

quiz.stem: Integrating reduction with the cell method, a leftover another player could rebuild should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Still explain the riff: cell, grouping, pedal; no invented I–V

distractors.text: Explain a chorale exam, even if that exam needs extra voices
distractors.rationale: The exam is the second piece.

distractors.text: Drop the cell and keep only genre adjectives as the leftover
distractors.rationale: Adjectives do not rebuild a riff.

distractors.text: Convert every pedal into a dominant so function can resume
distractors.rationale: A pedal is a wall, not an automatic V.

quiz.correctExplanation: Rebuildable leftover. Same riff. No rescue cadence.
objectiveIds: Leave a reduction that still explains the riff

lessons.title: Gain adds partials to the fifth
explanation: Gain is a harmonic fact. Distortion adds partials and intermodulation products. A clean fifth is two letters. The same fifth under drive is a crowd: extra harmonics, difference tones, a thickening that can make a missing third seem present. Report that crowd as harmony.

Predict why a fifth becomes a crowd: the spectrum of each string is already harmonic; clipping multiplies those spectra and sums them. Close intervals get harsher because their extra partials beat. Wide, simple intervals (octave, fifth) stay readable longer, which is why the power chord survives gain that would mud a cluster.

Write the same E5 clean, then driven. The letter did not change. The harmonic stack did. A chart that treats both as identical 'E5' is incomplete. Note the gain as part of the voicing, the way you would note an added seventh that was actually fingered.
lessons.example: Clean E5: E and B. Same frets, amp driven: a thicker stack, sometimes a ghost G, more beat frequencies if a neighbor F is added. The fifth became a crowd without a new fret.
lessons.whyItMatters: Ignore gain and you will wonder why a voicing that worked clean turns to mud driven. The extra partials were the missing voices.

quiz.stem: Treating gain as a harmonic fact means you should report which change?
quiz.correctAnswer: Added partials and intermodulation, not just a louder coat of paint

distractors.text: A new fret, because gain cannot add spectrum without new letters
distractors.rationale: The same frets can grow a crowd.

distractors.text: A tempo lift, because distortion is a rhythmic device here
distractors.rationale: The fact is spectral, not metric.

distractors.text: A mute of the fifth, because drive legally deletes pitch
distractors.rationale: Drive thickens the fifth. It does not delete it.

quiz.correctExplanation: Clipping adds partials. That is harmony on the same frets.
objectiveIds: Treat gain as a harmonic fact that adds partials

quiz.stem: Why does a fifth become a crowd under distortion while staying readable longer than a cluster?
quiz.correctAnswer: Clipping multiplies spectra; simple intervals' extra partials beat less than packed seconds

distractors.text: Gain retunes the B string up a third so a triad is fingered for you
distractors.rationale: No new fret appears. The third can be a ghost in the spectrum.

distractors.text: Fifth and cluster behave identically, because drive flattens all intervals
distractors.rationale: Packed seconds mud sooner. That is the prediction.

distractors.text: The crowd is only loudness, so interval packing cannot matter
distractors.rationale: Loudness is energy. The crowd is extra partials.

quiz.correctExplanation: Simple ratio, thicker spectrum. Packed seconds, harsher beats.
objectiveIds: Predict why a fifth becomes a crowd under distortion

quiz.stem: Clean E5 and driven E5 on the same frets. Distinguishing them as harmony means you should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Keep the letter and note the thicker partial stack as part of the voicing

distractors.text: Rename the driven take as a new chord because gain always changes the root
distractors.rationale: The root can sit. The stack grew.

distractors.text: Call them identical in every dimension, including spectrum
distractors.rationale: The letter matches. The partials do not.

distractors.text: Treat the driven take as a meter change into a denser bar
distractors.rationale: Spectrum changed. Grouping need not.

quiz.correctExplanation: Same letters, new crowd. Write the gain into the voicing report.
objectiveIds: Predict why a fifth becomes a crowd under distortion

lessons.title: Lowered sixth, power chord one finger
explanation: Drop a sixth string a whole step and a power chord becomes one finger: 0-0-0 on the bottom in drop D is D–A–D. The physics is a longer or slacker string whose open pitch is now a fifth below the fifth string, matching the power-chord shape. Write for that shape. Do not pretend the old E-standard fingering still applies.

Predict what the new open string does to pedals and cells. You now have a drone a whole step lower, easier unison chugs, and a fifth that can be barred across three strings. Chromatic cells still work, but their lowest wall moved. A riff that leaned on open E as pedal has a new wall at D, or C, or wherever you dropped.

Lower, then write a one-finger fifth, a pedal on the new open, and a cell that grinds against it. If you only drop the sixth and keep the old cells, you retuned a riff and left the new wall unused. The harmonic choice is the open string as a drone and a one-finger stack.
lessons.example: Drop D. One finger at the fifth fret is G–D–G. Open strings pedal D. A cell G–Ab–G now grinds against that D wall, which E-standard open E would not have given you for free.
lessons.whyItMatters: Treat drop tuning as a fashion and you will ignore the new wall. Treat it as physics and the pedal and the one-finger fifth are waiting.

quiz.stem: Lowering a string so a power chord is one finger, and writing for that physics, means you should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Use the new fifth-shape and the new open as material, not the old fingering

distractors.text: Keep E-standard shapes and ignore that the sixth string changed pitch
distractors.rationale: The sixth is a new letter. Write for it.

distractors.text: Mute the sixth string forever, because drop tunings ban open notes
distractors.rationale: The open string is the new wall.

distractors.text: Raise the other five strings to match, cancelling the drop
distractors.rationale: Cancelling the drop erases the physics.

quiz.correctExplanation: One-finger fifths. New open pitch. That is the writing.
objectiveIds: Lower a string so a power chord is one finger, and write for that physics

quiz.stem: Predict what the new open string does to pedals and cells in a drop tuning:
quiz.correctAnswer: A lower drone wall, easier unison chugs, and cells that grind against that new 0

distractors.text: Nothing, because open strings cannot pedal after a drop
distractors.rationale: The new 0 is often a better pedal.

distractors.text: An automatic V–I, because lower strings always cadence
distractors.rationale: A lower wall is not a dominant.

distractors.text: A mandatory 7/8, because drop tunings rewrite meter
distractors.rationale: Tuning is pitch physics, not grouping.

quiz.correctExplanation: New wall, new unisons, same cells possible against a different 0.
objectiveIds: Predict what the new open string does to pedals and cells

quiz.stem: You drop to D but keep an E-standard riff that never uses the sixth string. Identify the unused choice:
quiz.correctAnswer: The new open wall and the one-finger fifth were available and left idle

distractors.text: The drop secretly rewrote the riff's meter, so the idle string still counts
distractors.rationale: Meter did not move. The sixth did.

distractors.text: Idle sixths are required, because one-finger fifths are illegal
distractors.rationale: The one-finger fifth is the point of the drop.

distractors.text: The riff became Locrian automatically, so the sixth is now a diminished tonic
distractors.rationale: Tuning is not a mode assignment.

quiz.correctExplanation: If the new 0 never sounds, you retuned without taking the harmonic choice.
objectiveIds: Predict what the new open string does to pedals and cells
